docs.title: Training & Adjoints
docs.text: Training a learned solver means differentiating through an inner optimisation loop, and how you do that determines memory cost and gradient quality. The adjoint strategies here make that choice explicit and swappable — see Adjoint Methods in the Mathematical Reference for the trade-offs. Around them sit the loss functions and train/eval steps for 4DVarNet and the amortized posteriors, and the ConvLSTM gradient modulators that 4DVarNet learns in place of a hand-tuned inner optimiser.

docs.title: Adjoint strategies
docs.text:
Implementations of vardax.adjoints (Decision D15): full backpropagation with checkpointed memory (RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint), truncated one-step gradients (OneStepAdjoint, pairing with the one_step_solve_* solver functions), and implicit differentiation at a fixed point (ImplicitAdjoint, pairing with solve_4dvarnet_1d_fixedpoint). All three are also accessible via the vardax.adjoints submodule namespace. Use assert_adjoint_calibrated to verify a cheap adjoint against the exact one before trusting it.

RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint and ImplicitAdjoint are re-exported from optimistix for one-stop import; see the optimistix documentation for their full signatures:

  • vardax.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint — optimistix.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint, exact reverse-mode backpropagation through the unrolled inner loop with binomial checkpointing (the default).
  • vardax.ImplicitAdjoint — optimistix.ImplicitAdjoint, implicit-function-theorem differentiation at a fixed point; pair with solve_4dvarnet_1d_fixedpoint.

KStepAdjoint(k) is vardax's own truncated adjoint — warmup under stop_gradient, then k differentiable steps; OneStepAdjoint is the k=1 alias (Bolte, Pauwels & Vaiter, NeurIPS 2023):

vardax — Modular variational data assimilation with learned components.

All public symbols are re-exported from the private _src subpackage so that user code imports from the top-level namespace:

import vardax

model = vardax.FourDVarNet1D(...)

docs.title: KStepAdjoint
docs.text:
Bases: KStep

Deprecated alias of argminax.adjoint.KStep; use that name instead.

Building one emits a DeprecationWarning naming the argminax class; the alias is removed in the next release. It keeps vardax's contract (a ConfigurationError for k < 1, get_config / from_config) and inherits argminax's apply, so it now works under any optimistix solve. What follows describes the estimator, which is unchanged.

K-step differentiation: warmup under stop_gradient, then k live steps.

x^(j+1) = g_step(x^(j); θ),   j = 0, …, N_iter − 1
dx^(N_iter) / dθ ≈ ∂ g_stepᵏ(x^(N_iter − k); θ) / ∂θ

g_step is one iteration of the inner solver, and the iterate x^(N_iter − k) after the warmup is held fixed, so the gradient flows only through the last k steps. Memory for the backward pass is O(k) whatever the total iteration count, and at a converged fixed point the estimator is exact for any k, since the warmup iterations contribute nothing. For unconverged, truncated solvers, the 4DVarNet regime, a larger k trades memory for a less biased gradient. Use it as the solver_adjoint of FourDVarNet1D or FourDVarNet2D.

Algorithm
  1. Run the first N_iter − k solver iterations under jax.lax.stop_gradient.
  2. Run the last k iterations differentiably.
  3. Backpropagate through those k iterations only.

Attributes:

Name Type Description k

Number of trailing solver iterations that propagate gradients. Must be at least 1; values larger than n_solver_steps are clipped to a fully differentiable solve.

Raises:

Type Description ConfigurationError

If k is below 1.

Examples:

>>> import vardax
>>> vardax.KStepAdjoint(k=3)
KStepAdjoint(k=3)

k=1 is the one-step estimator, and OneStepAdjoint is a subclass.

>>> isinstance(vardax.OneStepAdjoint(), vardax.KStepAdjoint)
True
>>> vardax.KStepAdjoint().k
1

A non-positive k is rejected.

>>> vardax.KStepAdjoint(k=0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ConfigurationError: KStepAdjoint needs k >= 1; got k=0.
References

Bolte, J., Pauwels, E. & Vaiter, S. (2023). One-step differentiation of iterative algorithms. NeurIPS 36. arXiv:2305.13768.

class KStepAdjoint(KStep):
    """Deprecated alias of ``argminax.adjoint.KStep``; use that name instead.

    Building one emits a ``DeprecationWarning`` naming the argminax class; the
    alias is removed in the next release. It keeps vardax's contract (a
    ``ConfigurationError`` for ``k < 1``, ``get_config`` / ``from_config``) and
    inherits argminax's ``apply``, so it now works under any optimistix solve.
    What follows describes the estimator, which is unchanged.

    K-step differentiation: warmup under ``stop_gradient``, then ``k`` live steps.

        x^(j+1) = g_step(x^(j); θ),   j = 0, …, N_iter − 1
        dx^(N_iter) / dθ ≈ ∂ g_stepᵏ(x^(N_iter − k); θ) / ∂θ

    g_step is one iteration of the inner solver, and the iterate x^(N_iter − k) after
    the warmup is held fixed, so the gradient flows only through the last k steps.
    Memory for the backward pass is O(k) whatever the total iteration count, and at a
    converged fixed point the estimator is exact for any k, since the warmup
    iterations contribute nothing. For unconverged, truncated solvers, the 4DVarNet
    regime, a larger k trades memory for a less biased gradient. Use it as the
    ``solver_adjoint`` of [`FourDVarNet1D`][vardax.FourDVarNet1D] or
    [`FourDVarNet2D`][vardax.FourDVarNet2D].

    Algorithm:
        1. Run the first N_iter − k solver iterations under
           ``jax.lax.stop_gradient``.
        2. Run the last k iterations differentiably.
        3. Backpropagate through those k iterations only.

    Attributes:
        k: Number of trailing solver iterations that propagate gradients. Must be at
            least 1; values larger than ``n_solver_steps`` are clipped to a fully
            differentiable solve.

    Raises:
        ConfigurationError: If ``k`` is below 1.

    Examples:
        >>> import vardax
        >>> vardax.KStepAdjoint(k=3)
        KStepAdjoint(k=3)

        ``k=1`` is the one-step estimator, and `OneStepAdjoint` is a subclass.

        >>> isinstance(vardax.OneStepAdjoint(), vardax.KStepAdjoint)
        True
        >>> vardax.KStepAdjoint().k
        1

        A non-positive ``k`` is rejected.

        >>> vardax.KStepAdjoint(k=0)  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        ConfigurationError: KStepAdjoint needs k >= 1; got k=0.

    References:
        Bolte, J., Pauwels, E. & Vaiter, S. (2023). One-step differentiation of
        iterative algorithms. NeurIPS 36.
        [arXiv:2305.13768](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13768).
    """

    def __check_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.k < 1:
            raise ConfigurationError(f"KStepAdjoint needs k >= 1; got k={self.k}.")
        warn_renamed(type(self).__name__, _REPLACEMENT[type(self).__name__])

    def __repr__(self) -> str:  # pragma: no cover - cosmetic
        """Return ``KStepAdjoint(k=...)``."""
        return f"KStepAdjoint(k={self.k})"

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Return the fields needed to rebuild the adjoint."""
        return {
            "k": self.k,
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, config: dict[str, Any]) -> KStepAdjoint:
        """Rebuild an adjoint from ``get_config``."""
        return cls(**config)

to_optimistix_adjoint(spec: Any) -> AbstractAdjoint

Map an adjoint spec onto an optimistix.AbstractAdjoint.

Specs are matched structurally by class name, so identically named classes from other libraries are accepted interchangeably.

Algorithm
  1. Return spec unchanged if it already is an optimistix.AbstractAdjoint.
  2. Otherwise match it by class name against the mapping below.
  3. Raise for names that have no inner-solve counterpart.

Mapping:

  • ImplicitAdjoint() → optx.ImplicitAdjoint() — exact at a converged fixed point, O(1) memory, one Hessian linear solve.
  • RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint(checkpoints) → optx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint(checkpoints) — exact, recomputing.
  • TruncatedAdjoint(k) → KStepAdjoint(k) — warmup under stop_gradient, then k differentiable steps (k=1 is OneStepAdjoint).
  • DirectAdjoint / BacksolveAdjoint → UnsupportedInputError: the first is the plain unrolled default (pass optx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint() or nothing), the second only exists at the dynamics layer.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spec Any

A spec from pipekit_cycle.adjoints or any structurally identical object. A ready-made optx.AbstractAdjoint passes through unchanged.

required

Returns:

Type Description AbstractAdjoint

The corresponding optimistix adjoint instance.

Raises:

Type Description UnsupportedInputError

For layer-inappropriate or unrecognised specs.

>>> import optimistix as optx
>>> from pipekit_cycle.adjoints import TruncatedAdjoint
>>> from vardax.adjoints import to_optimistix_adjoint
>>> to_optimistix_adjoint(TruncatedAdjoint(k=3))
KStepAdjoint(k=3)
>>> isinstance(
...     to_optimistix_adjoint(optx.ImplicitAdjoint()), optx.ImplicitAdjoint
... )

A pipekit TruncatedAdjoint(k=1) is the one-step estimator, as a KStepAdjoint with k=1 rather than the OneStepAdjoint subclass.

>>> import vardax
>>> adjoint = to_optimistix_adjoint(TruncatedAdjoint(k=1))
>>> isinstance(adjoint, vardax.OneStepAdjoint)
False
>>> isinstance(adjoint, vardax.KStepAdjoint)
True

A spec with no inner-solve meaning is rejected.

>>> from pipekit_cycle.adjoints import DirectAdjoint
>>> to_optimistix_adjoint(DirectAdjoint())

def to_optimistix_adjoint(spec: Any) -> optx.AbstractAdjoint:
    """Map an adjoint spec onto an ``optimistix.AbstractAdjoint``.

    Specs are matched structurally by class name, so identically named classes from
    other libraries are accepted interchangeably.

    Algorithm:
        1. Return ``spec`` unchanged if it already is an
           ``optimistix.AbstractAdjoint``.
        2. Otherwise match it by class name against the mapping below.
        3. Raise for names that have no inner-solve counterpart.

    Mapping:

    - ``ImplicitAdjoint()`` → ``optx.ImplicitAdjoint()`` — exact at a
      converged fixed point, O(1) memory, one Hessian linear solve.
    - ``RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint(checkpoints)`` →
      ``optx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint(checkpoints)`` — exact,
      recomputing.
    - ``TruncatedAdjoint(k)`` →
      [`KStepAdjoint(k)`][vardax.adjoints.KStepAdjoint] — warmup under
      ``stop_gradient``, then ``k`` differentiable steps (``k=1`` is
      [`OneStepAdjoint`][vardax.adjoints.OneStepAdjoint]).
    - ``DirectAdjoint`` / ``BacksolveAdjoint`` →
      [`UnsupportedInputError`][vardax.UnsupportedInputError]: the
      first is the plain unrolled default (pass
      ``optx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint()`` or nothing), the second
      only exists at the dynamics layer.

    Args:
        spec: A spec from ``pipekit_cycle.adjoints`` or any
            structurally identical object. A ready-made
            ``optx.AbstractAdjoint`` passes through unchanged.

    Returns:
        The corresponding optimistix adjoint instance.

    Raises:
        UnsupportedInputError: For layer-inappropriate or unrecognised specs.

    Examples:
        >>> import optimistix as optx
        >>> from pipekit_cycle.adjoints import TruncatedAdjoint
        >>> from vardax.adjoints import to_optimistix_adjoint
        >>> to_optimistix_adjoint(TruncatedAdjoint(k=3))
        KStepAdjoint(k=3)
        >>> isinstance(
        ...     to_optimistix_adjoint(optx.ImplicitAdjoint()), optx.ImplicitAdjoint
        ... )
        True

        A pipekit ``TruncatedAdjoint(k=1)`` is the one-step estimator, as a
        ``KStepAdjoint`` with ``k=1`` rather than the `OneStepAdjoint` subclass.

        >>> import vardax
        >>> adjoint = to_optimistix_adjoint(TruncatedAdjoint(k=1))
        >>> isinstance(adjoint, vardax.OneStepAdjoint)
        False
        >>> isinstance(adjoint, vardax.KStepAdjoint)
        True

        A spec with no inner-solve meaning is rejected.

        >>> from pipekit_cycle.adjoints import DirectAdjoint
        >>> to_optimistix_adjoint(DirectAdjoint())  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        UnsupportedInputError: DirectAdjoint does not apply at the inner-solve layer
    """
    if isinstance(spec, optx.AbstractAdjoint):
        return spec
    name = type(spec).__name__
    try:
        # argminax matches the spec by name and owns the mapping
        adjoint = argminax_to_optimistix_adjoint(spec)
    except ValueError as error:
        if name in ("DirectAdjoint", "BacksolveAdjoint"):
            raise UnsupportedInputError(
                f"{name} does not apply at the inner-solve layer: DirectAdjoint is "
                "the plain unrolled default (use optx.RecursiveCheckpointAdjoint() "
                "or omit solver_adjoint), and BacksolveAdjoint only exists at the "
                "dynamics layer (see pipekit_jax.DiffraxForwardModel)."
            ) from error
        raise UnsupportedInputError(f"Unrecognised adjoint spec: {spec!r}") from error
    if type(adjoint) is KStep:
        # vardax's own name, as before; built quietly, since the caller asked for
        # a spec mapping and not for the deprecated class
        with warnings.catch_warnings():
            warnings.simplefilter("ignore", DeprecationWarning)
            return KStepAdjoint(k=adjoint.k)
    return adjoint

docs.text:
The learned components of 4DVarNet: ConvLSTM cells that map the raw variational-cost gradient to a descent update, satisfying the GradModulator Protocol. Their recurrent state is carried in the LSTMState1D / LSTMState2D containers.

vardax — Modular variational data assimilation with learned components.

All public symbols are re-exported from the private _src subpackage so that user code imports from the top-level namespace:

docs.title: ConvLSTMGradMod1D
docs.text:
Bases: Module

1-D ConvLSTM gradient modulator.

g_mod: (∇ₓ𝒥, x, c) ↦ (Δx, c′),   c = (c_hid, c_cell)
[a_in; a_forget; a_cand; a_out] = W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x] + W_hid c_hid
c_cell′ = σ(a_forget) ⊙ c_cell + σ(a_in) ⊙ tanh(a_cand)
c_hid′ = σ(a_out) ⊙ tanh(c_cell′)
Δx = W_out c_hid′

The carry c holds the LSTM hidden and cell states, σ is the logistic sigmoid, and W_in, W_hid and W_out are convolutions.

Algorithm
  1. Stack the gradient over the state along the channel axis and apply W_in; add W_hid applied to the hidden state.
  2. Split into the input, forget, candidate and output activations.
  3. Update the cell state c_cell′ and the hidden state c_hid′.
  4. Map c_hid′ back to the state channels with W_out.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state_channels int

Number of channels in the state and gradient (T).

required hidden_dim int

Number of hidden channels in the LSTM.

required kernel_size int

1-D convolution kernel size.

3 key PRNGKeyArray

PRNG key for the convolution weights.

required

Examples:

The update has the shape of the gradient, the carry the shape of the hidden state:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> mod = vdx.ConvLSTMGradMod1D(
...     state_channels=3, hidden_dim=5, key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
... )
>>> grad = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
>>> update, lstm = mod(grad, grad, vdx.LSTMState1D.zeros(2, 5, 4))
>>> update.shape, lstm.hidden.shape
((2, 3, 4), (2, 5, 4))

The carry persists across solver steps, so a second call with the returned carry gives a different update:

>>> update2, _ = mod(grad, grad, lstm)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(update, update2))
False

It conforms to the GradModulator protocol:

>>> isinstance(mod, vdx.GradModulator)
True

        ... )
        >>> grad = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
        >>> update, lstm = mod(grad, grad, vdx.LSTMState1D.zeros(2, 5, 4))
        >>> update.shape, lstm.hidden.shape
        ((2, 3, 4), (2, 5, 4))

        The carry persists across solver steps, so a second call with the returned
        carry gives a different update:

        >>> update2, _ = mod(grad, grad, lstm)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(update, update2))
        False

        It conforms to the [`GradModulator`][vardax.GradModulator] protocol:

        >>> isinstance(mod, vdx.GradModulator)
        True
    """

    state_channels: int = eqx.field(static=True)
    hidden_dim: int = eqx.field(static=True)
    kernel_size: int = eqx.field(static=True)
    _gates_input_conv: eqx.nn.Conv1d
    _gates_hidden_conv: eqx.nn.Conv1d
    _output_conv: eqx.nn.Conv1d

    def __init__(
        self,
        state_channels: int,
        hidden_dim: int,
        kernel_size: int = 3,
        *,
        key: PRNGKeyArray,
    ) -> None:
        self.state_channels = state_channels
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.kernel_size = kernel_size
        key_input, key_hidden, key_output = jax.random.split(key, 3)
        # an odd kernel keeps the spatial size
        padding = kernel_size // 2
        self._gates_input_conv = eqx.nn.Conv1d(
            in_channels=2 * state_channels,
            out_channels=4 * hidden_dim,
            kernel_size=kernel_size,
            padding=padding,
            key=key_input,
        )
        self._gates_hidden_conv = eqx.nn.Conv1d(
            in_channels=hidden_dim,
            out_channels=4 * hidden_dim,
            kernel_size=kernel_size,
            padding=padding,
            key=key_hidden,
        )
        self._output_conv = eqx.nn.Conv1d(
            in_channels=hidden_dim,
            out_channels=state_channels,
            kernel_size=kernel_size,
            padding=padding,
            key=key_output,
        )

    def __call__(
        self,
        grad: Float[Array, "B T N"],
        state: Float[Array, "B T N"],
        lstm_state: LSTMState1D,
    ) -> tuple[Float[Array, "B T N"], LSTMState1D]:
        """Turn a cost gradient into a state update: (Δx, c′) = g_mod(∇ₓ𝒥, x, c).

        Args:
            grad: Variational-cost gradient ∇ₓ𝒥.
            state: Current state x.
            lstm_state: Carry c = (c_hid, c_cell) with ``hidden_dim`` channels.

        Returns:
            The state update Δx and the new carry c′.
        """

        # eqx.nn.Conv1d takes (channels, space), and the arrays already have the
        # channels second (T for the gradient and state, H for the carry), so only
        # the batch axis needs a vmap
        def modulate_sample(
            grad_sample: Float[Array, "T N"],
            state_sample: Float[Array, "T N"],
            hidden_sample: Float[Array, "H N"],
            cell_sample: Float[Array, "H N"],
        ) -> tuple[Float[Array, "T N"], Float[Array, "H N"], Float[Array, "H N"]]:
            # [∇ₓ𝒥; x]
            stacked_input = einx.id("a n, b n -> (a + b) n", grad_sample, state_sample)
            # W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x]
            input_term = self._gates_input_conv(stacked_input)
            # W_hid c_hid
            hidden_term = self._gates_hidden_conv(hidden_sample)
            # [a_in; a_forget; a_cand; a_out] = W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x] + W_hid c_hid
            activations = input_term + hidden_term
            input_logit, forget_logit, candidate_logit, output_logit = einx.id(
                "(gate h) n -> gate h n", activations, gate=4
            )
            # σ(a_in)
            input_gate = jax.nn.sigmoid(input_logit)
            # σ(a_forget)
            forget_gate = jax.nn.sigmoid(forget_logit)
            # tanh(a_cand)
            cell_candidate = jnp.tanh(candidate_logit)
            # σ(a_out)
            output_gate = jax.nn.sigmoid(output_logit)
            # c_cell′ = σ(a_forget) ⊙ c_cell + σ(a_in) ⊙ tanh(a_cand)
            new_cell = forget_gate * cell_sample + input_gate * cell_candidate
            # c_hid′ = σ(a_out) ⊙ tanh(c_cell′)
            new_hidden = output_gate * jnp.tanh(new_cell)
            # Δx = W_out c_hid′
            update = self._output_conv(new_hidden)
            return update, new_hidden, new_cell

        update, new_hidden, new_cell = jax.vmap(modulate_sample)(
            grad, state, lstm_state.hidden, lstm_state.cell
        )
        return update, LSTMState1D(hidden=new_hidden, cell=new_cell)

Bases: Module

2-D ConvLSTM gradient modulator.

g_mod: (∇ₓ𝒥, x, c) ↦ (Δx, c′),   c = (c_hid, c_cell)
[a_in; a_forget; a_cand; a_out] = W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x] + W_hid c_hid
c_cell′ = σ(a_forget) ⊙ c_cell + σ(a_in) ⊙ tanh(a_cand)
c_hid′ = σ(a_out) ⊙ tanh(c_cell′)
Δx = W_out c_hid′

The same recurrence as ConvLSTMGradMod1D, with 2-D convolutions: the carry c holds the LSTM hidden and cell states, σ is the logistic sigmoid, and W_in, W_hid and W_out are convolutions.

Algorithm
  1. Stack the gradient over the state along the channel axis and apply W_in; add W_hid applied to the hidden state.
  2. Split into the input, forget, candidate and output activations.
  3. Update the cell state c_cell′ and the hidden state c_hid′.
  4. Map c_hid′ back to the state channels with W_out.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default state_channels int

Number of time channels in the state and gradient.

required hidden_dim int

Number of hidden channels in the LSTM.

required kernel_size int

2-D convolution kernel size.

3 key PRNGKeyArray

PRNG key for the convolution weights.

required

Examples:

The update has the shape of the gradient:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> mod = vdx.ConvLSTMGradMod2D(
...     state_channels=3, hidden_dim=2, key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
... )
>>> grad = jnp.ones((1, 3, 4, 5))
>>> update, lstm = mod(grad, grad, vdx.LSTMState2D.zeros(1, 2, 4, 5))
>>> update.shape, lstm.cell.shape
((1, 3, 4, 5), (1, 2, 4, 5))

A zero gradient and zero state still yield a finite update:

>>> zeros = jnp.zeros((1, 3, 4, 5))
>>> out, _ = mod(zeros, zeros, vdx.LSTMState2D.zeros(1, 2, 4, 5))
>>> bool(jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(out)))
True

It conforms to the GradModulator protocol:

>>> isinstance(mod, vdx.GradModulator)
True

class ConvLSTMGradMod2D(eqx.Module):
    """2-D ConvLSTM gradient modulator.

        g_mod: (∇ₓ𝒥, x, c) ↦ (Δx, c′),   c = (c_hid, c_cell)
        [a_in; a_forget; a_cand; a_out] = W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x] + W_hid c_hid
        c_cell′ = σ(a_forget) ⊙ c_cell + σ(a_in) ⊙ tanh(a_cand)
        c_hid′ = σ(a_out) ⊙ tanh(c_cell′)
        Δx = W_out c_hid′

    The same recurrence as [`ConvLSTMGradMod1D`][vardax.ConvLSTMGradMod1D], with 2-D
    convolutions: the carry c holds the LSTM hidden and cell states, σ is the logistic
    sigmoid, and W_in, W_hid and W_out are convolutions.

    Algorithm:
        1. Stack the gradient over the state along the channel axis and apply W_in;
           add W_hid applied to the hidden state.
        2. Split into the input, forget, candidate and output activations.
        3. Update the cell state c_cell′ and the hidden state c_hid′.
        4. Map c_hid′ back to the state channels with W_out.

    Args:
        state_channels: Number of time channels in the state and gradient.
        hidden_dim: Number of hidden channels in the LSTM.
        kernel_size: 2-D convolution kernel size.
        key: PRNG key for the convolution weights.

    Examples:
        The update has the shape of the gradient:

        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> mod = vdx.ConvLSTMGradMod2D(
        ...     state_channels=3, hidden_dim=2, key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
        ... )
        >>> grad = jnp.ones((1, 3, 4, 5))
        >>> update, lstm = mod(grad, grad, vdx.LSTMState2D.zeros(1, 2, 4, 5))
        >>> update.shape, lstm.cell.shape
        ((1, 3, 4, 5), (1, 2, 4, 5))

        A zero gradient and zero state still yield a finite update:

        >>> zeros = jnp.zeros((1, 3, 4, 5))
        >>> out, _ = mod(zeros, zeros, vdx.LSTMState2D.zeros(1, 2, 4, 5))
        >>> bool(jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(out)))
        True

        It conforms to the [`GradModulator`][vardax.GradModulator] protocol:

        >>> isinstance(mod, vdx.GradModulator)
        True
    """

    state_channels: int = eqx.field(static=True)
    hidden_dim: int = eqx.field(static=True)
    kernel_size: int = eqx.field(static=True)
    _gates_input_conv: eqx.nn.Conv2d
    _gates_hidden_conv: eqx.nn.Conv2d
    _output_conv: eqx.nn.Conv2d

    def __init__(
        self,
        state_channels: int,
        hidden_dim: int,
        kernel_size: int = 3,
        *,
        key: PRNGKeyArray,
    ) -> None:
        self.state_channels = state_channels
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.kernel_size = kernel_size
        key_input, key_hidden, key_output = jax.random.split(key, 3)
        # an odd kernel keeps the spatial size
        padding = kernel_size // 2
        self._gates_input_conv = eqx.nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels=2 * state_channels,
            out_channels=4 * hidden_dim,
            kernel_size=kernel_size,
            padding=padding,
            key=key_input,
        )
        self._gates_hidden_conv = eqx.nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels=hidden_dim,
            out_channels=4 * hidden_dim,
            kernel_size=kernel_size,
            padding=padding,
            key=key_hidden,
        )
        self._output_conv = eqx.nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels=hidden_dim,
            out_channels=state_channels,
            kernel_size=kernel_size,
            padding=padding,
            key=key_output,
        )

    def __call__(
        self,
        grad: Float[Array, "B T H W"],
        state: Float[Array, "B T H W"],
        lstm_state: LSTMState2D,
    ) -> tuple[Float[Array, "B T H W"], LSTMState2D]:
        """Turn a cost gradient into a state update: (Δx, c′) = g_mod(∇ₓ𝒥, x, c).

        Args:
            grad: Variational-cost gradient ∇ₓ𝒥.
            state: Current state x.
            lstm_state: Carry c = (c_hid, c_cell) with ``hidden_dim`` channels.

        Returns:
            The state update Δx and the new carry c′.
        """

        def modulate_sample(
            grad_sample: Float[Array, "T H W"],
            state_sample: Float[Array, "T H W"],
            hidden_sample: Float[Array, "H_dim H W"],
            cell_sample: Float[Array, "H_dim H W"],
        ) -> tuple[
            Float[Array, "T H W"],
            Float[Array, "H_dim H W"],
            Float[Array, "H_dim H W"],
        ]:
            # [∇ₓ𝒥; x]
            stacked_input = einx.id(
                "a h w, b h w -> (a + b) h w", grad_sample, state_sample
            )
            # W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x]
            input_term = self._gates_input_conv(stacked_input)
            # W_hid c_hid
            hidden_term = self._gates_hidden_conv(hidden_sample)
            # [a_in; a_forget; a_cand; a_out] = W_in [∇ₓ𝒥; x] + W_hid c_hid
            activations = input_term + hidden_term
            input_logit, forget_logit, candidate_logit, output_logit = einx.id(
                "(gate c) h w -> gate c h w", activations, gate=4
            )
            # σ(a_in)
            input_gate = jax.nn.sigmoid(input_logit)
            # σ(a_forget)
            forget_gate = jax.nn.sigmoid(forget_logit)
            # tanh(a_cand)
            cell_candidate = jnp.tanh(candidate_logit)
            # σ(a_out)
            output_gate = jax.nn.sigmoid(output_logit)
            # c_cell′ = σ(a_forget) ⊙ c_cell + σ(a_in) ⊙ tanh(a_cand)
            new_cell = forget_gate * cell_sample + input_gate * cell_candidate
            # c_hid′ = σ(a_out) ⊙ tanh(c_cell′)
            new_hidden = output_gate * jnp.tanh(new_cell)
            # Δx = W_out c_hid′
            update = self._output_conv(new_hidden)
            return update, new_hidden, new_cell

        update, new_hidden, new_cell = jax.vmap(modulate_sample)(
            grad, state, lstm_state.hidden, lstm_state.cell
        )
        return update, LSTMState2D(hidden=new_hidden, cell=new_cell)

def reconstruction_loss(
    pred: Float[Array, ...],
    target: Float[Array, ...],
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Mean-squared reconstruction loss.

        ℒ_MSE(x̂, x) = mean((x̂ − x)²)

    Args:
        pred: Model prediction x̂.
        target: Ground-truth target x, broadcastable against ``pred``.

    Returns:
        Scalar mean-squared error ℒ_MSE.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> prediction = jnp.array([1.0, 3.0])
        >>> float(vdx.reconstruction_loss(prediction, jnp.array([1.0, 1.0])))
        2.0

        A perfect prediction has zero loss, whatever the shape:

        >>> x = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
        >>> float(vdx.reconstruction_loss(x, x))
        0.0
    """
    # ℒ_MSE = mean((x̂ − x)²)
    return jnp.mean((pred - target) ** 2)

def train_loss_fn(
    model: Any,
    batch: Batch1D | Batch2D,
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Compute the training loss for a single batch.

        ℒ_MSE = mean((x̂ − x)²),   x̂ = model(batch),   x = batch.target

    Algorithm:
        1. Run the model on the batch to obtain the prediction x̂.
        2. Compare it with the target x using
           [`reconstruction_loss`][vardax.reconstruction_loss].

    Args:
        model: Equinox module implementing ``__call__(batch) -> prediction``.
        batch: Training batch (must have a non-``None`` ``target``).

    Returns:
        Scalar reconstruction loss.

    Raises:
        MissingInputError: If ``batch.target`` is ``None``.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import optax
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> model = vdx.FourDVarNet1D(
        ...     state_dim=4,
        ...     n_time=3,
        ...     latent_dim=2,
        ...     hidden_dim=3,
        ...     n_solver_steps=1,
        ...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
        ... )
        >>> ones = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
        >>> batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=ones, mask=ones, target=jnp.zeros((2, 3, 4)))
        >>> vdx.train_loss_fn(model, batch).shape
        ()

        It differentiates with respect to the model, as ``train_step`` does:

        >>> import equinox as eqx
        >>> loss, grads = eqx.filter_value_and_grad(vdx.train_loss_fn)(model, batch)
        >>> bool(jnp.isfinite(loss))
        True

        A batch without a target is rejected:

        >>> unlabelled = vdx.Batch1D(input=ones, mask=ones)
        >>> vdx.train_loss_fn(model, unlabelled)  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        MissingInputError: train_loss_fn requires batch.target to be set.
    """
    # x̂ = model(batch)
    prediction = model(batch)
    target = batch.target
    if target is None:
        raise MissingInputError("train_loss_fn requires batch.target to be set.")
    # ℒ_MSE = mean((x̂ − x)²)
    return reconstruction_loss(prediction, target)

Perform a single training step (forward, backward and update).

θ⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾ = θ⁽ⁱ⁾ + Δθ⁽ⁱ⁾,   (Δθ⁽ⁱ⁾, s⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾) = optimiser(∇_θ ℒ_MSE(θ⁽ⁱ⁾), s⁽ⁱ⁾)

with s the optimiser state. Gradients flow through the FourDVarNet inner solver according to the model's solver_adjoint. Compose this step into a notebook-level loop or pipekit_train.TrainingLoop rather than reimplementing it.

Algorithm
  1. Evaluate train_loss_fn and its gradient ∇_θ ℒ_MSE with respect to the model parameters θ.
  2. Turn the gradient into an update Δθ with the optax optimiser.
  3. Apply the update to the model.

Equinox module to optimise.

Training batch.

Current optimiser state.

required

The updated model, the updated optimiser state and the scalar loss

OptState

(evaluated before the update).

If batch.target is None.

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import equinox as eqx
>>> import optax
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> model = vdx.FourDVarNet1D(
...     state_dim=4,
...     n_time=3,
...     latent_dim=2,
...     hidden_dim=3,

>>> optimizer = optax.adam(1e-2)
>>> opt_state = optimizer.init(eqx.filter(model, eqx.is_array))
>>> new_model, opt_state, loss = vdx.train_step(
...     model, batch, optimizer, opt_state
... )
>>> loss.shape
()

The step returns the pre-update loss, so it equals eval_step on the old model, and the parameters have moved:

>>> bool(jnp.allclose(loss, vdx.eval_step(model, batch)))
True
>>> bool(eqx.tree_equal(new_model, model))
False

@eqx.filter_jit
def train_step(
    model: Any,
    batch: Batch1D | Batch2D,
    optimizer: optax.GradientTransformation,
    opt_state: optax.OptState,
) -> tuple[Any, optax.OptState, Float[Array, ""]]:
    """Perform a single training step (forward, backward and update).

        θ⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾ = θ⁽ⁱ⁾ + Δθ⁽ⁱ⁾,   (Δθ⁽ⁱ⁾, s⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾) = optimiser(∇_θ ℒ_MSE(θ⁽ⁱ⁾), s⁽ⁱ⁾)

    with s the optimiser state. Gradients flow through the FourDVarNet inner
    solver according to the model's ``solver_adjoint``. Compose this step into a
    notebook-level loop or ``pipekit_train.TrainingLoop`` rather than
    reimplementing it.

    Algorithm:
        1. Evaluate [`train_loss_fn`][vardax.train_loss_fn] and its gradient
           ∇_θ ℒ_MSE with respect to the model parameters θ.
        2. Turn the gradient into an update Δθ with the optax optimiser.
        3. Apply the update to the model.

    Args:
        model: Equinox module to optimise.
        batch: Training batch.
        optimizer: Optax gradient transformation (e.g. ``optax.adam(1e-3)``).
        opt_state: Current optimiser state.

    Returns:
        The updated model, the updated optimiser state and the scalar loss
        (evaluated before the update).

    Raises:
        MissingInputError: If ``batch.target`` is ``None``.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import equinox as eqx
        >>> import optax
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> model = vdx.FourDVarNet1D(
        ...     state_dim=4,
        ...     n_time=3,
        ...     latent_dim=2,
        ...     hidden_dim=3,
        ...     n_solver_steps=1,
        ...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
        ... )
        >>> ones = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
        >>> batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=ones, mask=ones, target=jnp.zeros((2, 3, 4)))
        >>> optimizer = optax.adam(1e-2)
        >>> opt_state = optimizer.init(eqx.filter(model, eqx.is_array))
        >>> new_model, opt_state, loss = vdx.train_step(
        ...     model, batch, optimizer, opt_state
        ... )
        >>> loss.shape
        ()

        The step returns the pre-update loss, so it equals ``eval_step`` on the
        old model, and the parameters have moved:

        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(loss, vdx.eval_step(model, batch)))
        True
        >>> bool(eqx.tree_equal(new_model, model))
        False
    """
    # ℒ_MSE(θ⁽ⁱ⁾) and ∇_θ ℒ_MSE(θ⁽ⁱ⁾)
    loss, grads = eqx.filter_value_and_grad(train_loss_fn)(model, batch)
    # Δθ⁽ⁱ⁾ from the optimiser
    updates, opt_state = optimizer.update(grads, opt_state, model)
    # θ⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾ = θ⁽ⁱ⁾ + Δθ⁽ⁱ⁾
    model = eqx.apply_updates(model, updates)
    return model, opt_state, loss

def amortized_nll_loss_fn(
    model: Any,
    batch: Batch1D | Batch2D,
) -> Float[Array, ""]:
    """Negative log-likelihood for amortized inference.

        ℒ_NLL(ν) = −mean(log q(x | y; ν))

    averaged over the simulated pairs (x, y) of the batch, for an
    ``AmortizedPosterior`` with any head that has a ``.log_prob``.

    Algorithm:
        1. Evaluate log q(x | y; ν) for each sample with
           ``model.log_prob(batch.target, batch)``.
        2. Return the negative batch mean.

    Args:
        model: ``AmortizedPosterior`` (any head with a ``.log_prob``
            method).
        batch: Training batch with ``target = x`` and ``input = y``.

    Returns:
        Scalar NLL averaged over the batch.

    Raises:
        MissingInputError: If ``batch.target`` is ``None``.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import optax
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
        >>> posterior = vdx.AmortizedPosterior(
        ...     encoder=vdx.MLPObsEncoder(input_size=12, context_dim=6, key=key),
        ...     head=vdx.RegressionHead(context_dim=6, state_shape=(3, 4), key=key),
        ...     config=vdx.AmortizedConfig(),
        ... )
        >>> ones = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
        >>> batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=ones, mask=ones, target=jnp.zeros((2, 3, 4)))
        >>> vdx.amortized_nll_loss_fn(posterior, batch).shape
        ()

        It is the negative mean of the per-sample log-density:

        >>> expected = -jnp.mean(posterior.log_prob(batch.target, batch))
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(vdx.amortized_nll_loss_fn(posterior, batch), expected))
        True

        The true state is required:

        >>> blind = vdx.Batch1D(input=ones, mask=ones)
        >>> vdx.amortized_nll_loss_fn(
        ...     posterior, blind
        ... )  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        MissingInputError: amortized_nll_loss_fn requires batch.target ...
    """
    target = batch.target
    if target is None:
        raise MissingInputError(
            "amortized_nll_loss_fn requires batch.target (the true x) to be set."
        )
    # log q(x | y; ν) per sample
    log_prob = model.log_prob(target, batch)
    # ℒ_NLL = −mean(log q(x | y; ν))
    return -jnp.mean(log_prob)

def amortized_train_step(
    model: Any,
    batch: Batch1D | Batch2D,
    optimizer: optax.GradientTransformation,
    opt_state: optax.OptState,
) -> tuple[Any, optax.OptState, Float[Array, ""]]:
    """Single training step for ``AmortizedPosterior``.

        ν⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾ = ν⁽ⁱ⁾ + Δν⁽ⁱ⁾,   (Δν⁽ⁱ⁾, s⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾) = optimiser(∇_ν ℒ_NLL(ν⁽ⁱ⁾), s⁽ⁱ⁾)

    [`amortized_nll_loss_fn`][vardax.amortized_nll_loss_fn] instead of the MSE
    reconstruction loss. Use this for simulation-based training of amortized
    variants; use ``train_step`` for ``FourDVarNet`` and classical models that
    reconstruct fields.

    Algorithm:
        1. Evaluate ℒ_NLL and its gradient ∇_ν ℒ_NLL with respect to the
           parameters ν.
        2. Turn the gradient into an update Δν with the optax optimiser.
        3. Apply the update to the model.

    Args:
        model: ``AmortizedPosterior`` to optimise.
        batch: Training batch with ``target = x`` and ``input = y``.
        optimizer: Optax gradient transformation.
        opt_state: Current optimiser state.

    Returns:
        The updated model, the updated optimiser state and the scalar NLL
        (evaluated before the update).

    Raises:
        MissingInputError: If ``batch.target`` is ``None``.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import optax
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> key = jax.random.PRNGKey(0)
        >>> posterior = vdx.AmortizedPosterior(
        ...     encoder=vdx.MLPObsEncoder(input_size=12, context_dim=6, key=key),
        ...     head=vdx.RegressionHead(context_dim=6, state_shape=(3, 4), key=key),
        ...     config=vdx.AmortizedConfig(),
        ... )
        >>> ones = jnp.ones((2, 3, 4))
        >>> batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=ones, mask=ones, target=jnp.zeros((2, 3, 4)))
        >>> import equinox as eqx
        >>> optimizer = optax.adam(1e-2)
        >>> opt_state = optimizer.init(eqx.filter(posterior, eqx.is_array))
        >>> new, opt_state, loss = vdx.amortized_train_step(
        ...     posterior, batch, optimizer, opt_state
        ... )
        >>> loss.shape
        ()

        A few steps reduce the loss on a fixed batch:

        >>> first = loss
        >>> for _ in range(5):
        ...     new, opt_state, loss = vdx.amortized_train_step(
        ...         new, batch, optimizer, opt_state
        ...     )
        >>> bool(loss < first)
        True
    """
    # ℒ_NLL(ν⁽ⁱ⁾) and ∇_ν ℒ_NLL(ν⁽ⁱ⁾)

    # ν⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾ = ν⁽ⁱ⁾ + Δν⁽ⁱ⁾
    model = eqx.apply_updates(model, updates)
    return model, opt_state, loss

Lorenz-63 vector field as an Equinox module.

ẋ = σ (y − x),   ẏ = x (ρ − z) − y,   ż = x y − β z

The module is a diffrax-compatible right-hand side f(t, y, args), whose y is the state (x, y, z).

Attributes:

Name Type Description sigma float

Prandtl number σ (classically 10).

rho float

Rayleigh number ρ (classically 28).

beta float

Geometric factor β (classically 8/3).

Examples:

The vector field at (1, 1, 1) for the classical parameters:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> f = vdx.Lorenz63(sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0)
>>> dydt = f(0.0, jnp.ones(3), None)
>>> (
...     dydt.shape,
...     bool(jnp.allclose(dydt, jnp.array([0.0, 26.0, 1.0 - 8.0 / 3.0]))),
... )
((3,), True)

The origin is a fixed point:

>>> bool(jnp.all(f(0.0, jnp.zeros(3), None) == 0))
True

It drives a DynTrajectory prior:

>>> ts = jnp.linspace(0.0, 0.05, 6)
>>> vdx.DynTrajectory(model=f)(jnp.ones(3), ts).shape
(6, 3)

class Lorenz63(eqx.Module):
    """Lorenz-63 vector field as an Equinox module.

        ẋ = σ (y − x),   ẏ = x (ρ − z) − y,   ż = x y − β z

    The module is a diffrax-compatible right-hand side ``f(t, y, args)``, whose
    ``y`` is the state (x, y, z).

    Attributes:
        sigma: Prandtl number σ (classically 10).
        rho: Rayleigh number ρ (classically 28).
        beta: Geometric factor β (classically 8/3).

    Examples:
        The vector field at (1, 1, 1) for the classical parameters:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> f = vdx.Lorenz63(sigma=10.0, rho=28.0, beta=8.0 / 3.0)
        >>> dydt = f(0.0, jnp.ones(3), None)
        >>> (
        ...     dydt.shape,
        ...     bool(jnp.allclose(dydt, jnp.array([0.0, 26.0, 1.0 - 8.0 / 3.0]))),
        ... )
        ((3,), True)

        The origin is a fixed point:

        >>> bool(jnp.all(f(0.0, jnp.zeros(3), None) == 0))
        True

        It drives a [`DynTrajectory`][vardax.DynTrajectory] prior:

        >>> ts = jnp.linspace(0.0, 0.05, 6)
        >>> vdx.DynTrajectory(model=f)(jnp.ones(3), ts).shape
        (6, 3)
    """

    sigma: float
    rho: float
    beta: float

    def __call__(
        self,
        t: float | Float[Array, ""],
        y: Float[Array, " 3"],
        args: None,
    ) -> Float[Array, " 3"]:
        """Evaluate the vector field at state ``y`` and time ``t``.

        Args:
            t: Time (unused; the system is autonomous).
            y: State (x, y, z).
            args: Unused, present for the diffrax signature.

        Returns:
            The time derivative (ẋ, ẏ, ż).
        """
        state_x, state_y, state_z = y[0], y[1], y[2]
        # ẋ = σ (y − x)
        dx_dt = self.sigma * (state_y - state_x)
        # ẏ = x (ρ − z) − y
        dy_dt = state_x * (self.rho - state_z) - state_y
        # ż = x y − β z
        dz_dt = state_x * state_y - self.beta * state_z
        return jnp.array([dx_dt, dy_dt, dz_dt])

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Return the parameters as a plain dictionary."""
        return {
            # float(): the parameters are leaves and may be 0-d arrays
            "sigma": float(self.sigma),
            "rho": float(self.rho),
            "beta": float(self.beta),
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, config: dict[str, Any]) -> Lorenz63:
        """Rebuild the module from ``get_config`` output."""
        return cls(**config)

Lorenz-96 vector field as an Equinox module.

ẋₙ = (xₙ₊₁ − xₙ₋₂) xₙ₋₁ − xₙ + F

with n indexing the sites of a periodic ring. The module is a diffrax-compatible right-hand side f(t, y, args), whose y is the state x.

Name Type Description forcing float

Forcing constant F (classically 8).

Examples:

The uniform state xₙ = F is a fixed point, and at the origin the field equals the forcing:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> f = vdx.Lorenz96(forcing=8.0)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(f(0.0, jnp.full(6, 8.0), None), 0.0))
True
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(f(0.0, jnp.zeros(6), None), 8.0))
True

It maps an N-vector to an N-vector, for any N:

>>> f(0.0, jnp.arange(5.0), None).shape
(5,)

It drives a DynTrajectory prior:

>>> ts = jnp.linspace(0.0, 0.05, 6)
>>> vdx.DynTrajectory(model=f)(jnp.arange(5.0), ts).shape

class Lorenz96(eqx.Module):
    """Lorenz-96 vector field as an Equinox module.

        ẋₙ = (xₙ₊₁ − xₙ₋₂) xₙ₋₁ − xₙ + F

    with n indexing the sites of a periodic ring. The module is a diffrax-compatible
    right-hand side ``f(t, y, args)``, whose ``y`` is the state x.

    Attributes:
        forcing: Forcing constant F (classically 8).

    Examples:
        The uniform state xₙ = F is a fixed point, and at the origin the field equals
        the forcing:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> f = vdx.Lorenz96(forcing=8.0)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(f(0.0, jnp.full(6, 8.0), None), 0.0))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(f(0.0, jnp.zeros(6), None), 8.0))
        True

        It maps an N-vector to an N-vector, for any N:

        >>> f(0.0, jnp.arange(5.0), None).shape
        (5,)

        It drives a [`DynTrajectory`][vardax.DynTrajectory] prior:

        >>> ts = jnp.linspace(0.0, 0.05, 6)
        >>> vdx.DynTrajectory(model=f)(jnp.arange(5.0), ts).shape
        (6, 5)
    """

    forcing: float

    def __call__(
        self,
        t: float | Float[Array, ""],
        y: Float[Array, " N"],
        args: None,
    ) -> Float[Array, " N"]:
        """Evaluate the vector field at state ``y`` and time ``t``.

        Args:
            t: Time (unused; the system is autonomous).
            y: State x on the periodic ring.
            args: Unused, present for the diffrax signature.

        Returns:
            The time derivative ẋ.
        """
        # xₙ₋₂
        back_two = jnp.roll(y, 2)
        # xₙ₋₁
        back_one = jnp.roll(y, 1)
        # xₙ₊₁
        ahead_one = jnp.roll(y, -1)
        # (xₙ₊₁ − xₙ₋₂) xₙ₋₁
        advection = (ahead_one - back_two) * back_one
        # ẋₙ = (xₙ₊₁ − xₙ₋₂) xₙ₋₁ − xₙ + F
        return advection - y + self.forcing

    def get_config(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        """Return the forcing as a plain dictionary."""
        return {
            # float(): the forcing is a leaf and may be a 0-d array
            "forcing": float(self.forcing),
        }

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, config: dict[str, Any]) -> Lorenz96:
        """Rebuild the module from ``get_config`` output."""
        return cls(**config)

def simulate_lorenz63(
    key: Array,
    *,
    sigma: float = 10.0,
    rho: float = 28.0,
    beta: float = 8.0 / 3.0,
    dt: float = 0.01,
    n_steps: int = 5000,
    n_burn_in: int = 1000,
    x0: Float[Array, " 3"] | None = None,
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " T"], Float[Array, "T 3"]]:
    """Simulate the Lorenz-63 system and return the state trajectory.

        ẋ = σ (y − x),   ẏ = x (ρ − z) − y,   ż = x y − β z

    Integrates the system with diffrax and discards a burn-in so the trajectory lies
    on the attractor.

    Algorithm:
        1. Build the initial condition, (1, 1, 1) perturbed by ``key``, or ``x0``.
        2. Integrate with ``Tsit5`` over ``n_burn_in + n_steps`` steps of size
           ``dt``, saving every step.
        3. Drop the first ``n_burn_in`` states and shift time to start at 0.

    Args:
        key: JAX PRNG key used to perturb the initial condition when ``x0`` is
            ``None``.
        sigma: Prandtl number σ.
        rho: Rayleigh number ρ.
        beta: Geometric factor β.
        dt: Integration time step.
        n_steps: Total number of integration steps after burn-in.
        n_burn_in: Number of initial steps to discard (burn-in).
        x0: Optional explicit initial condition x₀. When ``None``, the classic
            off-attractor point (1, 1, 1) is used, perturbed by ``key``. From there
            the transient onto the attractor takes a couple of time units, so the
            default burn-in lands on it. (Starting at the unstable fixed point
            instead, as older versions did, leaves the trajectory within a fraction
            of a unit of it for ~40 time units, far longer than any burn-in the
            tutorials use.)

    Returns:
        ``(time_coords, states)``: the time coordinates (starting at 0) and the
        Lorenz-63 state trajectory, with ``n_steps + 1`` rows.

    Examples:
        A short run without burn-in:

        >>> import jax
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> t, states = vdx.simulate_lorenz63(
        ...     jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_steps=10, n_burn_in=0
        ... )
        >>> t.shape, states.shape
        ((11,), (11, 3))
        >>> float(t[0])
        0.0

        An explicit initial condition is used as given:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> x0 = jnp.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
        >>> _, states = vdx.simulate_lorenz63(
        ...     jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_steps=5, n_burn_in=0, x0=x0
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(states[0], x0))
        True

        A burn-in is dropped from the output but the time axis restarts at 0:

        >>> t, states = vdx.simulate_lorenz63(
        ...     jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_steps=5, n_burn_in=5
        ... )
        >>> states.shape, float(t[0])
        ((6, 3), 0.0)
    """
    model = Lorenz63(sigma=sigma, rho=rho, beta=beta)

    if x0 is None:
        # x₀ = (1, 1, 1) + 0.01 ξ, ξ ~ 𝒩(0, I)
        noise = jax.random.normal(key, shape=(3,)) * 0.01
        x0 = jnp.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) + noise

    total_steps = n_burn_in + n_steps
    start_time = 0.0
    end_time = total_steps * dt

    save_times = jnp.linspace(start_time, end_time, total_steps + 1)

    solution = diffeqsolve(
        ODETerm(model),  # type: ignore[arg-type]  # ty:ignore[invalid-argument-type]
        Tsit5(),
        t0=start_time,
        t1=end_time,
        dt0=dt,
        y0=x0,
        saveat=SaveAt(ts=save_times),
        # Fixed-step integration takes exactly ``total_steps`` steps; diffrax's
        # default cap (4096) would abort long simulations (e.g. 5000 + 1000).
        max_steps=total_steps + 1,
    )

    # Discard burn-in steps; keep indices n_burn_in .. total_steps (inclusive)
    states = solution.ys[n_burn_in:]
    # tₖ − t_burn, so the time axis restarts at 0
    time_coords = save_times[n_burn_in:] - save_times[n_burn_in]
    return time_coords, states

def simulate_lorenz96(
    key: Array,
    *,
    n_sites: int = 40,
    forcing: float = 8.0,
    dt: float = 0.01,
    n_steps: int = 5000,
    n_burn_in: int = 1000,
) -> tuple[Float[Array, " T"], Float[Array, "T N"]]:
    """Simulate the Lorenz-96 system and return the state trajectory.

        ẋₙ = (xₙ₊₁ − xₙ₋₂) xₙ₋₁ − xₙ + F

    Integrates the system on a periodic ring with diffrax and discards a burn-in.

    Algorithm:
        1. Start from the uniform state xₙ = F plus a small perturbation drawn from
           ``key``.
        2. Integrate with ``Tsit5`` over ``n_burn_in + n_steps`` steps of size
           ``dt``, saving every step.
        3. Drop the first ``n_burn_in`` states and shift time to start at 0.

    Args:
        key: JAX PRNG key used to perturb the initial condition.
        n_sites: Number of variables (spatial dimension).
        forcing: Forcing constant F.
        dt: Integration time step.
        n_steps: Total number of integration steps after burn-in.
        n_burn_in: Number of initial steps to discard (burn-in).

    Returns:
        ``(time_coords, states)``: the time coordinates (starting at 0) and the
        state trajectory, with ``n_steps + 1`` rows.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> t, states = vdx.simulate_lorenz96(
        ...     jax.random.PRNGKey(0), n_sites=8, n_steps=10, n_burn_in=0
        ... )
        >>> t.shape, states.shape
        ((11,), (11, 8))

        The perturbation of the initial state depends on the key:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> _, other = vdx.simulate_lorenz96(
        ...     jax.random.PRNGKey(1), n_sites=8, n_steps=10, n_burn_in=0
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(states[0], other[0]))
        False

        The result feeds a plotting helper directly:

        >>> import matplotlib
        >>> import numpy as np
        >>> matplotlib.use("Agg")
        >>> fig, ax = vdx.plot_l96_grid(np.asarray(states), np.asarray(t))
        >>> type(ax).__name__
        'Axes'
    """
    model = Lorenz96(forcing=forcing)

    # the standard L96 start: x₀,ₙ = F + 0.01 ξₙ, ξₙ ~ 𝒩(0, 1)
    initial_state = jnp.full((n_sites,), forcing)
    noise = jax.random.normal(key, shape=(n_sites,)) * 0.01
    initial_state = initial_state + noise

    total_steps = n_burn_in + n_steps
    start_time = 0.0
    end_time = total_steps * dt

    save_times = jnp.linspace(start_time, end_time, total_steps + 1)

    solution = diffeqsolve(
        ODETerm(model),  # type: ignore[arg-type]  # ty:ignore[invalid-argument-type]
        Tsit5(),
        t0=start_time,
        t1=end_time,
        dt0=dt,
        y0=initial_state,
        saveat=SaveAt(ts=save_times),
        # Fixed-step integration takes exactly ``total_steps`` steps; diffrax's
        # default cap (4096) would abort long simulations (e.g. 5000 + 1000).
        max_steps=total_steps + 1,
    )

    states = solution.ys[n_burn_in:]
    # tₖ − t_burn, so the time axis restarts at 0
    time_coords = save_times[n_burn_in:] - save_times[n_burn_in]
    return time_coords, states

def time_patches(ts: Float[Array, " T"]) -> Float[Array, "T-1 2"]:
    """Overlapping consecutive time pairs for one-step increment losses.

        (tᵢ, tᵢ₊₁),   i = 0, …, T − 2

    Reimplements the legacy ``kernex.kmap(kernel_size=(2,), relative=True)`` sliding
    window without the ``kernex`` dependency.

    Args:
        ts: Monotonic time coordinates t₀, …, t_(T−1).

    Returns:
        The consecutive pairs (tᵢ, tᵢ₊₁), one row per pair.

    Examples:
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> from vardax import time_patches
        >>> pairs = time_patches(jnp.arange(4.0))
        >>> pairs.shape, pairs.tolist()
        ((3, 2), [[0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0], [2.0, 3.0]])

        A single time yields no pairs:

        >>> time_patches(jnp.array([0.0])).shape
        (0, 2)

        The pairs drive the one-step solves of
        [`DynIncrements`][vardax.DynIncrements]:

        >>> time_patches(jnp.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 5)).shape
        (4, 2)
    """
    # jnp, not einx: a single time gives zero pairs, which einx cannot size
    return jnp.stack([ts[:-1], ts[1:]], axis=-1)

SoftBoundedForward wraps any pipekit_cycle.ForwardModel so that the line search of a variational solver cannot drive an explicit ODE step off the attractor into overflow: inside a box the adapter is the identity, outside it saturates smoothly. Notebooks 13 and 14 use it around Lorenz-96 and Lorenz-63 forwards.

vardax — Modular variational data assimilation with learned components.

All public symbols are re-exported from the private _src subpackage so that user code imports from the top-level namespace:

import vardax

model = vardax.FourDVarNet1D(...)

docs.text:
Bases: Module

ForwardModel adapter that softly confines states to a box.

xₜ = s(f(s(xₜ₋₁)))
s(x) = x                             for |x| ≤ b
s(x) = sign(x) (b + b u / (1 + u))   for |x| > b,   u = (|x| − b) / b

Explicit Runge–Kutta steps of dynamics with quadratic terms (Lorenz-63, Lorenz-96, …) overflow, or drive an adaptive step-size controller past its step cap, when the state is far outside the attractor. A line-search minimiser such as the BFGS inside StrongFourDVar will try such states, and one non-finite cost is enough to poison the whole solve. This adapter maps the state through s on the way into and out of every step, so that

  • states inside the box |xᵢ| ≤ b are untouched (choose bound so the attractor sits well inside it; the adapter is then exactly the wrapped model wherever the analysis can end up);
  • states outside are confined to |xᵢ| < 2b, keeping every trial cost finite;
  • the map is continuously differentiable (slope one at the box edge from both sides) and its gradient outside, 1 / (1 + u)², stays representable in single precision for trial states up to about 10¹⁹ times the bound, unlike a hard clip (zero gradient) or a tanh saturation (gradient underflows to zero a few bounds out); a rejected trial therefore still carries curvature information if the minimiser asks for it.
Algorithm
  1. Confine the incoming state with s.
  2. Advance it with the wrapped model's step, f.
  3. Confine the result with s again.

Attributes:

Name Type Description forward Any

The wrapped pipekit_cycle.ForwardModel, f.

bound float

Half-width b of the box on which the adapter is the identity.

Examples:

Inside the box the state is untouched, and far outside it is confined:

>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import vardax
>>> class Double:
...     dt = 1.0
...     state_signature = None
...
...     def step(self, x, dt):
...         return 2.0 * x
>>> fwd = vardax.SoftBoundedForward(Double(), bound=10.0)
>>> stepped = fwd.step(jnp.array([1.0, -3.0]), 1.0)
>>> bool(jnp.allclose(stepped, jnp.array([2.0, -6.0])))
True
>>> bool(jnp.all(jnp.abs(fwd.step(jnp.array([1e6, -1e6]), 1.0)) < 20.0))
True

The step length and signature are forwarded from the wrapped model:

>>> fwd.dt, fwd.state_signature
(1.0, None)

Wrapped around a diffrax-backed model it keeps a far-off state finite:

>>> def decay(t, y, args):
...     return -y
>>> inner = vardax.DynTrajectory(model=decay).as_forward_model(0.1)
>>> safe = vardax.SoftBoundedForward(inner, bound=5.0)
>>> bool(jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(safe.step(jnp.array([1e9]), 0.1))))
True

class SoftBoundedForward(eqx.Module):
    """``ForwardModel`` adapter that softly confines states to a box.

        xₜ = s(f(s(xₜ₋₁)))
        s(x) = x                             for |x| ≤ b
        s(x) = sign(x) (b + b u / (1 + u))   for |x| > b,   u = (|x| − b) / b

    Explicit Runge–Kutta steps of dynamics with quadratic terms (Lorenz-63,
    Lorenz-96, …) overflow, or drive an adaptive step-size controller past its step
    cap, when the state is far outside the attractor. A line-search minimiser such
    as the BFGS inside [`StrongFourDVar`][vardax.StrongFourDVar] will try such
    states, and one non-finite cost is enough to poison the whole solve. This
    adapter maps the state through s on the way into and out of every step, so that

    - states inside the box |xᵢ| ≤ b are untouched (choose ``bound`` so the attractor
      sits well inside it; the adapter is then exactly the wrapped model wherever
      the analysis can end up);
    - states outside are confined to |xᵢ| < 2b, keeping every trial cost finite;
    - the map is continuously differentiable (slope one at the box edge from both
      sides) and its gradient outside, 1 / (1 + u)², stays representable in single
      precision for trial states up to about 10¹⁹ times the bound, unlike a hard clip
      (zero gradient) or a ``tanh`` saturation (gradient underflows to zero a few
      bounds out); a rejected trial therefore still carries curvature information
      if the minimiser asks for it.

    Algorithm:
        1. Confine the incoming state with s.
        2. Advance it with the wrapped model's ``step``, f.
        3. Confine the result with s again.

    Attributes:
        forward: The wrapped ``pipekit_cycle.ForwardModel``, f.
        bound: Half-width b of the box on which the adapter is the identity.

    Examples:
        Inside the box the state is untouched, and far outside it is confined:

        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import vardax
        >>> class Double:
        ...     dt = 1.0
        ...     state_signature = None
        ...
        ...     def step(self, x, dt):
        ...         return 2.0 * x
        >>> fwd = vardax.SoftBoundedForward(Double(), bound=10.0)
        >>> stepped = fwd.step(jnp.array([1.0, -3.0]), 1.0)
        >>> bool(jnp.allclose(stepped, jnp.array([2.0, -6.0])))
        True
        >>> bool(jnp.all(jnp.abs(fwd.step(jnp.array([1e6, -1e6]), 1.0)) < 20.0))
        True

        The step length and signature are forwarded from the wrapped model:

        >>> fwd.dt, fwd.state_signature
        (1.0, None)

        Wrapped around a diffrax-backed model it keeps a far-off state finite:

        >>> def decay(t, y, args):
        ...     return -y
        >>> inner = vardax.DynTrajectory(model=decay).as_forward_model(0.1)
        >>> safe = vardax.SoftBoundedForward(inner, bound=5.0)
        >>> bool(jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(safe.step(jnp.array([1e9]), 0.1))))
        True
    """

    forward: Any
    bound: float = eqx.field(static=True)

    @property
    def dt(self) -> float:
        """Step length of the wrapped model."""
        return self.forward.dt

    @property
    def state_signature(self) -> Any:
        """State signature of the wrapped model, or ``None`` if it has none."""
        return getattr(self.forward, "state_signature", None)

    def _confine(self, state: Array) -> Array:
        """Apply the confinement map s elementwise."""
        half_width = self.bound
        # |x|
        abs_state = jnp.abs(state)
        # The in-box branch returns ``state`` itself (not ``sign * abs``) so the
        # gradient is exactly one everywhere inside, including at zero, where
        # ``jnp.sign`` would otherwise zero it. Outside, the algebraic
        # saturation u / (1 + u) keeps the derivative 1 / (1 + u)² finite and
        # non-zero far beyond any state a line search will try (tanh would
        # underflow to a zero gradient a few bounds out).
        # u = max(|x| − b, 0) / b
        excess = jnp.maximum(abs_state - half_width, 0.0) / half_width
        # s(x) = sign(x) (b + b u / (1 + u))
        outside = jnp.sign(state) * (half_width + half_width * excess / (1.0 + excess))
        # s(x) = x where |x| ≤ b
        return jnp.where(abs_state <= half_width, state, outside)

    def step(self, state: Array, dt: float) -> Array:
        """Advance ``state`` by ``dt`` with confinement before and after.

        Args:
            state: State xₜ₋₁ to advance.
            dt: Step length Δt.

        Returns:
            xₜ = s(f(s(xₜ₋₁))), with f the wrapped model's step.
        """
        # s(xₜ₋₁)
        confined_state = self._confine(state)
        # f(s(xₜ₋₁))
        stepped_state = self.forward.step(confined_state, dt)
        # xₜ = s(f(s(xₜ₋₁)))
        return self._confine(stepped_state)

    Args:
        state: State xₜ₋₁ to advance.
        dt: Step length Δt.

    Returns:
        xₜ = s(f(s(xₜ₋₁))), with f the wrapped model's step.
    """
    # s(xₜ₋₁)
    confined_state = self._confine(state)
    # f(s(xₜ₋₁))
    stepped_state = self.forward.step(confined_state, dt)
    # xₜ = s(f(s(xₜ₋₁)))
    return self._confine(stepped_state)

docs.title: Validation gates
docs.text:
The six-step methodology's go/no-go checks (Decision D12): simulation-based calibration ranks the truth within posterior samples and must be uniform; assert_posterior_agreement cross-checks two posterior adapters against each other; and assert_adjoint_calibrated verifies that a cheap adjoint tracks the exact gradient before it is used for training. Run these before believing any uncertainty estimate.

vardax — Modular variational data assimilation with learned components.

All public symbols are re-exported from the private _src subpackage so that user code imports from the top-level namespace:

import vardax

model = vardax.FourDVarNet1D(...)

docs.text:
simulation_based_calibration(
    sample_posterior: Callable[
        [Array, PRNGKeyArray, int], Array
    ],
    sample_prior: Callable[[PRNGKeyArray], Array],
    simulate_obs: Callable[[Array, PRNGKeyArray], Array],
    *,
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
    n_runs: int = 200,
    n_samples: int = 200,
) -> Int[Array, " n_runs"]

Rank histogram of true draws within posterior samples (Talts et al. 2018).

rankₙ = |{e : ‖x⁽ᵉ⁾‖₂ < ‖xₙ‖₂}|,   x⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ q(x ∣ yₙ; ν),   xₙ ~ p(x)

with n indexing the n_runs independent runs and e the n_samples posterior samples. A well-calibrated posterior produces uniformly distributed ranks over [0, n_samples]; bumps near the edges mean over-confident, a bump at the centre means under-confident.

Algorithm
  1. For each run, split the key into prior, observation and posterior keys.
  2. Draw xₙ from the prior, simulate yₙ and draw the posterior samples x⁽ᵉ⁾.
  3. Reduce xₙ and every sample to its ℓ₂ norm.
  4. Record how many sample norms fall below the norm of xₙ.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sample_posterior Callable[[Array, PRNGKeyArray, int], Array]

(y, key, n) -> Array of posterior samples with n leading rows, conditioned on y. An AmortizedPosterior plugs in through a one-element batch, as in the last example.

required sample_prior Callable[[PRNGKeyArray], Array]

key -> x. Single prior draw xₙ.

required simulate_obs Callable[[Array, PRNGKeyArray], Array]

(x, key) -> y. Forward plus noise, yₙ.

required key PRNGKeyArray

Top-level PRNG key.

required n_runs int

Number of (prior, obs, posterior) triples.

200 n_samples int

Posterior samples per run (defines the rank histogram resolution).

200

Returns:

Type Description Int[Array, ' n_runs']

Integer ranks in [0, n_samples], one per run.

Examples:

Ranks of the truth among samples drawn around the observation lie in [0, n_samples]:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> prior = lambda k: jax.random.normal(k, (2,))
>>> observe = lambda x, k: x + 0.1 * jax.random.normal(k, (2,))
>>> posterior = lambda y, k, n: y + 0.1 * jax.random.normal(k, (n, 2))
>>> ranks = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(
...     posterior,
...     prior,
...     observe,
...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
...     n_runs=6,
...     n_samples=10,
... )
>>> ranks.shape, bool(jnp.all((ranks >= 0) & (ranks <= 10)))
((6,), True)

A posterior that ignores the data puts the truth below every sample, so every rank is zero:

>>> wrong = lambda y, k, n: 100.0 + jax.random.normal(k, (n, 2))
>>> bad = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(
...     wrong,
...     prior,
...     observe,
...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
...     n_runs=6,
...     n_samples=10,
... )
>>> bool(jnp.all(bad == 0))
True

An AmortizedPosterior plugs in through a one-element batch:

>>> key = jax.random.PRNGKey(1)
>>> amortized = vdx.AmortizedPosterior(
...     encoder=vdx.MLPObsEncoder(input_size=6, context_dim=4, key=key),
...     head=vdx.RegressionHead(context_dim=4, state_shape=(2, 3), key=key),
...     config=vdx.AmortizedConfig(),
... )
>>> import einx
>>> def sample_posterior(y, k, n):
...     window = einx.id("s... -> 1 s...", y)
...     batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=window, mask=jnp.ones_like(window))
...     return amortized.sample(batch, k, n)[0]
>>> ranks = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(
...     sample_posterior,
...     lambda k: jax.random.normal(k, (2, 3)),
...     lambda x, k: x,
...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(2),
...     n_runs=4,
...     n_samples=5,
... )
>>> ranks.shape
(4,)
References

Talts, Betancourt, Simpson, Vehtari & Gelman (2018). "Validating Bayesian inference algorithms with simulation-based calibration."

def simulation_based_calibration(
    sample_posterior: Callable[[Array, PRNGKeyArray, int], Array],
    sample_prior: Callable[[PRNGKeyArray], Array],
    simulate_obs: Callable[[Array, PRNGKeyArray], Array],
    *,
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
    n_runs: int = 200,
    n_samples: int = 200,
) -> Int[Array, " n_runs"]:
    """Rank histogram of true draws within posterior samples (Talts et al. 2018).

        rankₙ = |{e : ‖x⁽ᵉ⁾‖₂ < ‖xₙ‖₂}|,   x⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ q(x ∣ yₙ; ν),   xₙ ~ p(x)

    with n indexing the ``n_runs`` independent runs and e the ``n_samples`` posterior
    samples. A well-calibrated posterior produces uniformly distributed ranks over
    ``[0, n_samples]``; bumps near the edges mean over-confident, a bump at the centre
    means under-confident.

    Algorithm:
        1. For each run, split the key into prior, observation and posterior keys.
        2. Draw xₙ from the prior, simulate yₙ and draw the posterior samples x⁽ᵉ⁾.
        3. Reduce xₙ and every sample to its ℓ₂ norm.
        4. Record how many sample norms fall below the norm of xₙ.

    Args:
        sample_posterior: ``(y, key, n) -> Array`` of posterior samples with
            ``n`` leading rows, conditioned on ``y``. An ``AmortizedPosterior`` plugs
            in through a one-element batch, as in the last example.
        sample_prior: ``key -> x``. Single prior draw xₙ.
        simulate_obs: ``(x, key) -> y``. Forward plus noise, yₙ.
        key: Top-level PRNG key.
        n_runs: Number of (prior, obs, posterior) triples.
        n_samples: Posterior samples per run (defines the rank histogram resolution).

    Returns:
        Integer ranks in ``[0, n_samples]``, one per run.

    Examples:
        Ranks of the truth among samples drawn around the observation lie in
        ``[0, n_samples]``:

        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> prior = lambda k: jax.random.normal(k, (2,))
        >>> observe = lambda x, k: x + 0.1 * jax.random.normal(k, (2,))
        >>> posterior = lambda y, k, n: y + 0.1 * jax.random.normal(k, (n, 2))
        >>> ranks = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(
        ...     posterior,
        ...     prior,
        ...     observe,
        ...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
        ...     n_runs=6,
        ...     n_samples=10,
        ... )
        >>> ranks.shape, bool(jnp.all((ranks >= 0) & (ranks <= 10)))
        ((6,), True)

        A posterior that ignores the data puts the truth below every sample, so
        every rank is zero:

        >>> wrong = lambda y, k, n: 100.0 + jax.random.normal(k, (n, 2))
        >>> bad = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(
        ...     wrong,
        ...     prior,
        ...     observe,
        ...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(0),
        ...     n_runs=6,
        ...     n_samples=10,
        ... )
        >>> bool(jnp.all(bad == 0))
        True

        An [`AmortizedPosterior`][vardax.AmortizedPosterior] plugs in through a
        one-element batch:

        >>> key = jax.random.PRNGKey(1)
        >>> amortized = vdx.AmortizedPosterior(
        ...     encoder=vdx.MLPObsEncoder(input_size=6, context_dim=4, key=key),
        ...     head=vdx.RegressionHead(context_dim=4, state_shape=(2, 3), key=key),
        ...     config=vdx.AmortizedConfig(),
        ... )
        >>> import einx
        >>> def sample_posterior(y, k, n):
        ...     window = einx.id("s... -> 1 s...", y)
        ...     batch = vdx.Batch1D(input=window, mask=jnp.ones_like(window))
        ...     return amortized.sample(batch, k, n)[0]
        >>> ranks = vdx.simulation_based_calibration(
        ...     sample_posterior,
        ...     lambda k: jax.random.normal(k, (2, 3)),
        ...     lambda x, k: x,
        ...     key=jax.random.PRNGKey(2),
        ...     n_runs=4,
        ...     n_samples=5,
        ... )
        >>> ranks.shape
        (4,)

    References:
        Talts, Betancourt, Simpson, Vehtari & Gelman (2018). "Validating Bayesian
        inference algorithms with simulation-based calibration."
    """
    keys = jax.random.split(key, n_runs)
    ranks = []
    for run_key in keys:
        prior_key, obs_key, posterior_key = jax.random.split(run_key, 3)
        # xₙ ~ p(x)
        true_state = sample_prior(prior_key)
        # yₙ = h(xₙ) + ε
        observation = simulate_obs(true_state, obs_key)
        # x⁽ᵉ⁾ ~ q(x ∣ yₙ; ν)
        samples = sample_posterior(observation, posterior_key, n_samples)
        # ‖xₙ‖₂ is the scalar reduction the rank compares
        true_norm = float(jnp.linalg.norm(true_state))
        # ‖x⁽ᵉ⁾‖₂² over every state dimension of each sample
        squared_norms = einx.sum("member [s...]", samples**2)
        # ‖x⁽ᵉ⁾‖₂
        sample_norms = jnp.sqrt(squared_norms)
        # rankₙ = |{e : ‖x⁽ᵉ⁾‖₂ < ‖xₙ‖₂}|
        rank = int(jnp.sum(sample_norms < true_norm))
        ranks.append(rank)
    return jnp.asarray(ranks, dtype=jnp.int32)

docs.title: assert_posterior_agreement
docs.text:
assert_posterior_agreement(
    p_fast: Posterior,
    p_oracle: Posterior,
    *,
    tolerance_sigma: float = 1.0,
) -> None

Check that the fast posterior mean lies near the oracle's, per component.

zᵢ = |μ_fast,i − μ_oracle,i| / σᵢ ≤ ``tolerance_sigma``,   σᵢ² = [Σ_x|y]ᵢᵢ

with Σ_x|y the oracle's posterior covariance. The test is marginal only. The diagonal comes from gaussx.diag, in closed form for a structured operator and by materialising a generic one, which is cheap for moderate state size; for very large state sizes use Hutchinson estimation upstream and supply the diagonal directly via Posterior.cov materialised as a diagonal operator.

Algorithm
  1. Extract the oracle marginal standard deviations σᵢ from p_oracle.cov.
  2. Compute the z-scores zᵢ from the mean difference μ_fast − μ_oracle.
  3. Fail if any zᵢ exceeds tolerance_sigma.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default p_fast Posterior

Posterior produced by the amortized or fast model, with mean μ_fast.

required p_oracle Posterior

Posterior produced by the oracle (e.g. StrongFourDVar + LaplaceCovariance), with mean μ_oracle.

required tolerance_sigma float

Allowed deviation in units of σᵢ.

1.0

Raises:

Type Description MissingInputError

If p_oracle.cov is None.

ShapeError

If the two means have different shapes.

AssertionError

If any component exceeds the tolerance.

Examples:

A fast mean within one oracle standard deviation passes silently:

>>> import jax
>>> import jax.numpy as jnp
>>> import lineax as lx
>>> import vardax as vdx
>>> cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((3,), jnp.float32))
>>> oracle = vdx.Posterior(mean=jnp.zeros(3), cov=cov)
>>> fast = vdx.Posterior(mean=jnp.array([0.5, -0.5, 0.0]))
>>> vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(fast, oracle, tolerance_sigma=1.0)

A deviation of three standard deviations fails:

>>> far = vdx.Posterior(mean=jnp.array([3.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
>>> vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(
...     far, oracle
... )
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
AssertionError: posterior agreement failed: max z = 3.000 > 1.000.

An oracle without a covariance cannot supply the scale:

>>> vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(
...     fast, fast
... )
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
MissingInputError: assert_posterior_agreement requires p_oracle.cov ...

def assert_posterior_agreement(
    p_fast: Posterior,
    p_oracle: Posterior,
    *,
    tolerance_sigma: float = 1.0,
) -> None:
    """Check that the fast posterior mean lies near the oracle's, per component.

        zᵢ = |μ_fast,i − μ_oracle,i| / σᵢ ≤ ``tolerance_sigma``,   σᵢ² = [Σ_x|y]ᵢᵢ

    with Σ_x|y the oracle's posterior covariance. The test is marginal only. The
    diagonal comes from ``gaussx.diag``, in closed form for a structured operator and
    by materialising a generic one, which is cheap for moderate state size; for very
    large state sizes use Hutchinson estimation upstream and supply the diagonal
    directly via ``Posterior.cov`` materialised as a diagonal operator.

    Algorithm:
        1. Extract the oracle marginal standard deviations σᵢ from ``p_oracle.cov``.
        2. Compute the z-scores zᵢ from the mean difference μ_fast − μ_oracle.
        3. Fail if any zᵢ exceeds ``tolerance_sigma``.

    Args:
        p_fast: Posterior produced by the amortized or fast model, with mean μ_fast.
        p_oracle: Posterior produced by the oracle (e.g. ``StrongFourDVar``
            + [`LaplaceCovariance`][vardax.LaplaceCovariance]), with mean μ_oracle.
        tolerance_sigma: Allowed deviation in units of σᵢ.

    Raises:
        MissingInputError: If ``p_oracle.cov`` is ``None``.
        ShapeError: If the two means have different shapes.
        AssertionError: If any component exceeds the tolerance.

    Examples:
        A fast mean within one oracle standard deviation passes silently:

        >>> import jax
        >>> import jax.numpy as jnp
        >>> import lineax as lx
        >>> import vardax as vdx
        >>> cov = lx.IdentityLinearOperator(jax.ShapeDtypeStruct((3,), jnp.float32))
        >>> oracle = vdx.Posterior(mean=jnp.zeros(3), cov=cov)
        >>> fast = vdx.Posterior(mean=jnp.array([0.5, -0.5, 0.0]))
        >>> vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(fast, oracle, tolerance_sigma=1.0)

        A deviation of three standard deviations fails:

        >>> far = vdx.Posterior(mean=jnp.array([3.0, 0.0, 0.0]))
        >>> vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(
        ...     far, oracle
        ... )  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        AssertionError: posterior agreement failed: max z = 3.000 > 1.000.

        An oracle without a covariance cannot supply the scale:

        >>> vdx.assert_posterior_agreement(
        ...     fast, fast
        ... )  # doctest: +IGNORE_EXCEPTION_DETAIL
        Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
        MissingInputError: assert_posterior_agreement requires p_oracle.cov ...
    """
    if p_oracle.cov is None:
        raise MissingInputError(
            "assert_posterior_agreement requires p_oracle.cov to be set "
            "(used to extract the marginal standard deviations)."
        )
    if p_fast.mean.shape != p_oracle.mean.shape:
        raise ShapeError(
            "p_fast.mean and p_oracle.mean must have the same shape; got "
            f"{p_fast.mean.shape} vs {p_oracle.mean.shape}."
        )
    oracle_std = _marginal_std(p_oracle.cov, p_oracle.mean)
    # zᵢ = |μ_fast,i − μ_oracle,i| / σᵢ, floored so a zero variance cannot divide by 0
    z_score = jnp.abs(p_fast.mean - p_oracle.mean) / jnp.maximum(oracle_std, 1e-12)
    if jnp.any(z_score > tolerance_sigma):
        worst = float(jnp.max(z_score))
        raise AssertionError(
            f"posterior agreement failed: max z = {worst:.3f} > {tolerance_sigma:.3f}."
        )
